reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Men describe orgasm with little or no antegrade ejaculate, and the first urine passed afterwards is characteristically cloudy from admixed semen
The diagnosis is confirmed by finding sperm in a post-orgasmic urine specimen, distinguishing it from failure of emission where no semen is produced at all
The common causes are diabetic autonomic neuropathy, bladder-neck or prostate surgery, retroperitoneal surgery, and alpha-blocker medication
It is a recognised and treatable cause of low-volume ejaculate and of male-factor infertility
Alkalinisation and appropriate preparation of the post-orgasmic urine allow sperm to be harvested for assisted reproduction when medical treatment fails
Medical treatment aims to restore bladder-neck closure using sympathomimetic or alpha-agonist agents, most useful when the cause is neuropathic rather than anatomical
Anatomical causes following bladder-neck resection generally do not respond to drugs, so assisted conception is planned from the outset when fertility is the goal
reference.pathophysiology: Normal ejaculation depends on coordinated closure of the bladder neck at the moment of emission so that semen is propelled forward through the urethra rather than back into the bladder. When the internal urethral sphincter fails to close, seminal fluid takes the path of least resistance and flows retrogradely into the bladder. This failure may be neurogenic, as in diabetic autonomic neuropathy or after retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection that interrupts sympathetic outflow; anatomical, following transurethral or open bladder-neck and prostate surgery that destroys the sphincter mechanism; or pharmacological, notably with alpha-adrenergic blocking drugs that relax the bladder neck. The result is a reduced or absent antegrade ejaculate with sperm recoverable from the post-orgasmic urine.
additionalDifferentials: Ejaculatory duct obstruction producing low ejaculate volume
Congenital absence of the vasa and seminal vesicles
additionalInvestigations: Post-orgasmic urine analysis for the presence of sperm, the confirmatory test
Standard semen analysis assessing ejaculate volume and sperm content
Blood glucose or HbA1c to identify diabetes
Medication review focusing on alpha-blockers and other implicated drugs
Surgical and neurological history including bladder-neck, prostate, and retroperitoneal procedures
Scrotal or transrectal ultrasound where an anatomical or obstructive cause is also considered
redFlags: New retrograde ejaculation as an early clue to undiagnosed diabetes
Recent retroperitoneal or pelvic surgery with additional neurological deficits
Associated bladder or voiding symptoms suggesting broader outflow pathology
Complete absence of orgasmic sensation pointing to a different neurological problem
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and does not threaten general health; fertility is frequently achievable, either by restoring antegrade ejaculation with medication in neuropathic cases or by retrieving sperm from post-orgasmic urine for assisted reproduction when the cause is anatomical.
pitfalls: Confusing retrograde ejaculation with true anejaculation by not examining post-orgasmic urine
Attempting drug treatment for an anatomical bladder-neck defect that will not respond
Missing underlying diabetes as the driver of a neuropathic cause
Overlooking a culprit alpha-blocker that could simply be adjusted
Failing to alkalinise and prepare urine promptly, reducing the yield of viable sperm
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
